node.label: Pat Thane
node.date_label: Foundations of the Welfare State (1982; second edition 1996) · Old Age in English History (2000) · Sinners? Scroungers? Saints?, with Tanya Evans (2012)
node.description: In Old Age in English History: Past Experiences, Present Issues (2000), Pat Thane argues that older people have long been visible, active contributors to English communities, challenging assumptions that they were uniformly dependent or supported by families alone. She treats later life as varied by resources, work, gender and personal circumstances, rather than a single experience of decline. Daniel Blackie praised the book’s account of older people’s agency but criticized its sketchier treatment of pre-industrial England and judged its modern sections stronger. Foundations of the Welfare State (1982; second edition 1996) belongs to her wider history of welfare provision. Her parliamentary Social Care memorandum (2009) traces the interdependence of state, voluntary and family support; with Tanya Evans she wrote Sinners? Scroungers? Saints? (2012), on unmarried motherhood in twentieth-century England. Her later work connects women’s unequal paid and caring work to poverty and representations in old age. With Janet Nelson and Penelope Corfield she helped establish the IHR Women’s History Seminar in 1986.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Foundations of the Welfare State (1982; second edition 1996); Old Age in English History: Past Experiences, Present Issues (2000); Women and Ageing in British Society since 1500 (2001), edited with Lynn Botelho; Sinners? Scroungers? Saints? Unmarried Motherhood in Twentieth-Century England (2012), with Tanya Evans; Divided Kingdom: A History of Britain, 1900 to the Present (2018).

proposed_edges.relationship: In a filmed IHR interview with Hobsbawm (catalogued c. 1988, though the transcript calls The Age of Empire, published 1987, 'shortly to come'), Thane questions him about Marxist historical explanation, Labouring Men (1964) and the relationship between working-class culture and labour institutions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: IHR catalogue, Video details: “Date of creation: c. 1988”; transcript PDF pp. 5–11, especially p. 10 at 00:17:47 and 00:19:15 and p. 11 at 00:20:01. This is a documented intellectual conversation, not evidence that Hobsbawm supervised Thane or that she adopted all his answers. Only the transcript portion was read; recording not viewed. Machine transcription warning retained. Original creation is approximate; 2025 is digitization/release. The distinct 1978–79 interview with Liz Lunbeck was found bibliographically but not read and is not used for its content.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kelly Boyd’s “The Women’s History Seminar” (2024) identifies Thane, Janet Nelson and Penelope Corfield as the scholars whose lobbying established the IHR Women’s History Seminar in 1986.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Background and founding, paragraphs beginning The founding of the Seminar and They included, then first-term account and notes 18–19. Named collaboration: “Janet (Jinty) Nelson, Pat Thane and Penelope (Penny) Corfield”. Boyd explicitly says the exact negotiations are not remembered; the edge claims joint founding work, not a reconstructed division of labour or personal intellectual influence. Nelson’s 2008 IHR interview corroborates her co-founder role but does not itself name Thane.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her June 1996 review of Hufton’s The Prospect Before Her (1995), Thane invokes Linda Colley’s warning that insistent prescriptions may signal challenges to the norms they announce, supporting the need to test prescriptive writing against other evidence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete review, paragraph beginning One of the strengths of the book and following paragraph on separate spheres. Thane attributes the point to “others, such as Linda Colley” and explains that prescription can be especially insistent when norms are challenged. This is a limited, explicit methodological uptake in this review, not a claim of formative influence, priority, or a uniquely Colley-derived method. Thane does not identify Colley’s particular work; it remains unidentified and unread. Hufton’s 1995 book also unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Old Age in English History (2000) makes older people’s varied work, resources and agency part of social history, challenging the assumption that they were uniformly dependent burdens.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read publisher abstract and contents, plus Blackie’s complete review, PDF pp. 1–2, especially paragraph beginning Another major achievement. Blackie stresses older people’s agency while criticizing thin pre-industrial treatment. This contribution is supported by publisher framing and a named scholarly reader; the book body remains unread. This route concerns social agency and inequality, distinct from the family-support question on the demography route.

proposed_edges.relationship: Boyd’s “The Women’s History Seminar” (2024) places Thane’s founding work for the IHR seminar in 1986 within the institutional expansion of women’s history and records her opening-term paper “Ideologies of Gender”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Background and founding and Establishing the Seminar: named lobbying, first full term beginning 6 June 1986 and Thane’s paper, then discussion of the seminar’s function as a forum for new research. “Ideologies of Gender” is identified by Boyd through Nelson’s diaries; the paper itself is unread and no argument is attributed to it. The edge concerns a documented contribution to the field, not membership or shared employment alone.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Gendered Narratives of Ageing in Britain since 1900” (2023), Thane connects older women’s poverty to unequal earnings and caring work, and argues that accounts of ageing often overlook women’s numerical predominance and varied contributions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read printed pp. 14–19 (Introduction, Incomes of Older Women, feminist neglect and pensions), pp. 23–29 (positive ageing, diversity, caring and paid/unpaid work). Opening diagnoses omission of the “predominantly female experience”; income section connects working lives and pensions. Later sections complicate uniform dependency narratives. Claims are restricted to the article’s historical argument; its statistical sources were not independently rechecked.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her Social Care memorandum (October 2009), Thane challenges romantic accounts of past family care, linking older people’s access to children’s support to mortality, non-marriage, infertility and emigration.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Memorandum PDF p. 4, Before 1939: Voluntary and Family Care, continuing onto p. 5: “Family care ... should not be romanticized”; she explicitly says the evidence is not systematic before listing demographic limits on available children. These pages were read directly. The edge connects history of the family and population to the mixed provision of care, not a claim that Thane developed a demographic reconstruction technique. Remaining memorandum pp. 9–15 not closely read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thane’s Social Care memorandum (October 2009), submitted to the House of Commons Health Committee, uses the history of public, voluntary and family care to explain the continuing difficulty of separating health care from chargeable social care.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Direct memorandum reading, PDF pp. 1–8: submission heading and author statement p. 1; summary pp. 1–2; care in the new welfare state pp. 6–7. Source says it was submitted to provide historical context to the committee. Landing posted December 2009, distinct from October submission. No claim about parliamentary adoption or policy impact is made; the separate REF impact-case fetch failed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Helen McCarthy credits Thane’s ‘What Difference Did the Vote Make?’ (2001) with showing how voluntary organisations encouraged female voters to recognise their collective political power and civic responsibilities, a contribution to the history of interwar political participation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the relevant body discussion and note 32 in McCarthy’s 2012 historiographical review on Cambridge Core. The attribution is shared with Beaumont and others; no exclusive priority is claimed. Thane’s original essay was not read. This records a specific contribution to political history; McCarthy has no eligible person endpoint.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thane’s ‘Women in the British Labour Party and the Construction of State Welfare, 1906–39’ (1993) contributed to maternal and infant welfare history through its account of philanthropy politicising women who pressed for state provision, an interpretation Linda Bryder explicitly draws upon.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the introduction and associated notes on Cambridge Core. Bryder also disputes Thane’s explanation of how welfare became a political issue, stressing campaigning alongside demographic fears. The original chapter was not read. The contribution concerns infant-welfare historiography, not medical practice. Bryder has no eligible person endpoint.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thane co-edited The Power of the Past: Essays for Eric Hobsbawm (1984), a Festschrift, with Geoffrey Crossick and Roderick Floud.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Crossref records for reviews of the book (e.g. Ira Katznelson, Journal of Modern History 60:2, 1988, DOI 10.1086/600347) give the editors as Thane, Crossick and Floud and the title 'The Power of the Past: Essays for Eric Hobsbawm'. Bibliographic evidence only; the volume was not read. Added from Fable's review (F07-019).
